english: for something to become urgent / for a deadline to be right on top of you (lit. 'fire falls on the top of your foot')
usage: 발등에 불 떨어져서 밤새 했어.
It got urgent at the last second, so I pulled an all-nighter.
Casual; 떨어지다 is past here as 떨어져서 ('because it fell')
마감이 코앞이라 이제 발등에 불 떨어졌어요.
The deadline's right there, so now it's crunch time.
Polite; pairs naturally with 코앞 ('right in front')
발등에 불 떨어져야 움직이는 스타일이야.
I only get moving once it's down to the wire.
-아야 = 'only when/once'; describes a procrastinator habit
발등에 불이 떨어졌는데 아직도 시작을 안 했어?
It's crunch time and you still haven't started?
Subject 이/가 often added: 불이 떨어지다
examples: A: 야, 발등에 불 떨어졌다, 마감이 내일이잖아! / B: 아, 진짜? 부랴부랴 해야겠다.
A: Hey, it's crunch time — the deadline is tomorrow! / B: Oh, for real? Gotta rush.
A/B exchange; 부랴부랴 ('in a frantic rush') is the natural partner adverb
발등에 불 떨어지고 나서야 짐을 부랴부랴 쌌어요.
Only when it became urgent did I hurriedly pack.
-고 나서야 = 'only after (something happened)'; classic procrastinator structure
다들 발등에 불 떨어진 듯이 회의실로 뛰어갔어.
Everyone ran to the meeting room like it was an emergency.
Group panic; -ㄴ 듯이 = 'as if'; describes the sudden scramble
nuance: Literally 'fire falls on the top of your foot (발등)' — when a live ember lands on your instep you jump instantly, so this paints a crisis that has suddenly arrived and demands you drop everything this second. The near-synonym 코앞이다 ('right in front of your nose') only states that a deadline is close in time; 발등에 불 떨어지다 adds the involuntary, panicked scramble of having to act right now, which is why it so naturally pairs with 부랴부랴 ('frantically') and 밤새다 ('pull an all-nighter'). It carries a wry, self-aware, procrastinator's tone — Koreans use 발등에 불 떨어져야 움직인다 ('I only move once the fire hits my foot') as an almost affectionate admission of leaving things to the last minute. The scale from casual to polite is very wide: 발등에 불 떨어졌어 (casual) through 발등에 불 떨어진 상황입니다 (formal briefing). The English-speaker pitfall: do not read 떨어지다 as 'runs out' — here it means the fire 'fell/dropped' onto you, so the crisis has arrived, not vanished; and 발등 is specifically the instep/top of the foot, not just 발 ('foot').

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'fire (불) falls (떨어지다) onto the instep of the foot (발등)' — like a hot ember landing on your foot, you jump instantly. In use it means a crisis or deadline has arrived so suddenly and pressingly that you must act this very second with no buffer left.

Fits any situation where something once distant is now breathing down your neck — work deadlines, paperwork, exams, event preparations. Casual (발등에 불 떨어졌어) to polite (발등에 불 떨어진 상황이에요) to formal written context. Safe to use with friends, colleagues, and bosses. Often tinged with self-deprecating humor about procrastinating.

코앞이다 ('right in front of one's nose') states that a deadline is close in time but without the bodily panic. 발등에 불 떨어지다 adds the involuntary scramble — things are urgent AND you must move right now. 급하다 ('to be urgent') is the plain adjective; this idiom dramatizes the same idea with vivid imagery.

Particles shift freely: 불이 떨어지다 (subject 이) or 불 떨어지다 (topic/zero). Common extensions: 발등에 불 떨어져서 밤새다 ('pull an all-nighter because it got urgent'), 발등에 불 떨어져야 움직이다 ('only move once the fire hits') for habitual procrastination.

Do not read 떨어지다 as 'run out' — here it means the fire 'fell/dropped' (crisis arrived), not 'ran out' (crisis ended). Also, 발등 is specifically the instep/top of the foot; dropping 등 removes the vivid image. Finally, this is not about injury — it is pure urgency metaphor.

mistakes: Don't read it literally as a burn injury — it is about sudden urgency, not pain, so 'My foot got burned' is a complete mis-hearing.
It's 발등 (the top/instep of the foot), not 발 ('foot') — drop 등 and the vivid image of an ember landing on the exposed instep is lost.
Keep 떨어지다 in the right direction: it means the fire FELL (the crisis is here), so don't confuse it with the meaning 'to run out / be used up.'

english: to be right around the corner / extremely close in time or distance (lit. 'it's right in front of your nose')
usage: 시험이 코앞이야, 큰일 났어.
The exam is right around the corner — I'm in trouble.
Casual; time sense, looming pressure
마감이 코앞이라 정신없어요.
The deadline's right on top of us, so it's hectic.
Polite; -이라 = 'since it is'; very common with 마감
편의점 코앞인데 귀찮아서 안 나가.
The convenience store is right there but I'm too lazy to go.
Distance sense — 'a stone's throw'
코앞에 두고도 못 찾았어.
It was right under my nose and I still couldn't find it.
코앞에 두다 = 'to have right in front of you'
examples: A: 이사 날짜 언제야? / B: 코앞이야, 이번 주 토요일.
A: When's the moving date? / B: Super soon — this Saturday.
A/B exchange; 이사 날짜 ('moving date') with time sense
설날이 코앞인데 기차표를 아직 못 구했어.
Lunar New Year is around the corner and I still can't get a train ticket.
Seasonal urgency; 구하다 = 'to secure/get'
회사가 집 코앞이라 걸어서 5분이면 가요.
The office is right by my place — five minutes on foot.
Distance sense: X 코앞이다 = 'right by X'
nuance: Literally 'right in front of the nose' (코 'nose' + 앞 'front'), 코앞이다 frames something as extremely near — either in TIME (an event or deadline almost upon you) or in DISTANCE (a place a few steps away). The dividing line from the neutral near-synonym 가깝다 ('to be close') is vividness and immediacy: 가깝다 is a measurable, unemotional word ('the station is near'), while 코앞이다 dramatizes 'practically touching your face,' loading on urgency for time and a 'no excuse not to go' feeling for distance. When time is the axis it typically pairs with pressure: 마감이 코앞이라 정신없어요. The compound 코앞 is written as one word, not 코 앞. Register is casual-to-polite and the expression is extremely common in everyday speech. The English-speaker pitfall: 'right under my nose' in English usually means 'I missed something obvious,' but plain Korean 코앞이다 just means 'very near' — the 'missed the obvious' shade only appears when context (e.g. 코앞에 두고도 못 찾다) supplies it explicitly.

structuredNuance.t: 코앞 = 코 ('nose') + 앞 ('front'), literally 'right in front of the nose.' In use it means something is extremely near — either in time (an imminent event or deadline) or in physical distance (a place just a few steps away). It dramatizes closeness with the vivid image of something nearly touching your face.

Used constantly in casual and polite speech alike. TIME sense: 마감/시험/이사 날짜가 코앞이다 — an event is almost here and you feel the pressure. DISTANCE sense: 편의점/회사가 코앞이다 — a place is so close it would be silly not to go. Safe with anyone; no formality issues.

가깝다 ('to be close') is the neutral, measurable word — 'the station is near.' 코앞이다 dramatizes the same idea: 'practically touching your face,' making it feel more pressing for time and more obvious-convenience for distance. 임박하다 is the formal written equivalent for time-proximity.
코앞에 두다 ('to have/leave something right in front of you'), 코앞에서 놓치다 ('to miss something right there'). Spatial formula: [place] 코앞에 [place 2] 있다 ('place 2 is right in front of place 1').

'Right under my nose' in English usually means 'I missed something obvious,' but Korean 코앞 plainly means 'very near.' The 'missed the obvious' shade only appears when context (e.g. 코앞에 두고도 못 찾다) explicitly supplies it. Also write it as one word: 코앞, not 코 앞.

mistakes: Write 코앞 as one word, not 코 앞 — it's a fixed compound noun.
Context decides whether it means 'soon' (time) or 'nearby' (distance); don't assume only the time reading, or you'll misread 집 코앞 ('right by the house').
Don't auto-map it to the English idiom 'right under my nose' (= 'missed something obvious'); plain 코앞이다 just means 'very close.'

english: to get chills down one's spine / be struck with fear or dread (lit. 'one's spine goes cold/shivery')
usage: 그 얘기 듣고 등골이 오싹했어.
I got chills down my spine hearing that.
Casual; fear/creepiness, past tense 오싹했어
밤에 혼자 그 길 걸으니까 등골이 오싹하더라고요.
Walking that road alone at night gave me the shivers.
Polite; -더라고요 reports a felt experience
사고 영상 보니까 등골이 다 오싹해.
Watching the accident footage sent a total chill down my spine.
다 here = 'completely,' intensifying the shiver
생각만 해도 등골이 서늘해.
Just thinking about it sends a chill down my back.
등골이 서늘하다 = close variant ('spine goes cool')
examples: A: 그 귀신 나오는 장면에서 어땠어? / B: 등골이 오싹해서 눈도 못 뜨겠더라.
A: How did you feel at the ghost scene? / B: I had chills down my spine and could barely open my eyes.
A/B exchange; horror-movie startle, 눈도 못 뜨겠더라 = 'could barely keep my eyes open'
하마터면 큰일 날 뻔했다고 생각하니 등골이 오싹해.
Thinking I almost got into real trouble gives me the chills.
하마터면 ~ㄹ 뻔하다 = 'almost (nearly) happened'; dread over a close call
그 사람 눈빛이 너무 차가워서 등골이 오싹했어요.
His gaze was so cold it sent a shiver down my spine.
Real-situation: an unsettling person, not weather cold; shows non-horror usage
nuance: 등골 is the spine or its marrow, and 오싹하다 is that sudden, involuntary cold-shudder, so together they capture the physical chill running down your back from fear, eeriness, or the retrospective dread of realizing you barely dodged disaster. It describes the bodily sensation rather than naming the emotion — which is why it is more vivid than just saying 무섭다 ('it's scary'). The near-synonym 등골이 서늘하다 ('spine goes cool') conveys a quieter, more lingering unease — a slow dread — while 등골이 오싹하다 is the sharp, sudden goose-bump spike from a sudden noise, revelation, or image. Use it for horror, ghost stories, near-miss anecdotes, and cold-eyed strangers. Register is casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfalls: this is fear-chills, NOT being physically cold from the weather (use 춥다 for that); the body-part partner 등골 collocates with 오싹하다 and 서늘하다 — 등골이 춥다 is unnatural; and note the romanization: 오싹 is the mimetic of a sudden shiver, so it also appears standalone as 오싹! when someone flinches.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 등골 ('spine/spinal marrow') + 오싹하다 ('to go cold and shivery in an instant'). 실제 뜻: the involuntary spine-chill you feel from fear, eeriness, or the retroactive dread of a near-miss — emphasizing the physical bodily reaction rather than the emotion itself.

Fits horror movies, ghost stories, a frightening news story, a creepy stranger's gaze, or realizing you barely avoided danger. Casual to polite; fine among friends and in storytelling contexts. Not used in formal writing — switch to 공포를 느끼다 in serious/formal prose.

등골이 서늘하다 ('spine goes cool') is the close variant — quieter, more lingering dread. 오싹하다 is the sharper spike from a sudden noise, image, or revelation. 무섭다 ('to be scared') names the emotion but gives no bodily sensation; 등골이 오싹하다 paints the physical shiver.
등골이 서늘하다 (slower chill/dread), 소름이 돋다 ('goosebumps rise' — same fear zone but on the skin surface), 오싹! as a standalone mimetic for a shiver. Intensifier: 등골이 다 오싹해 ('completely chilled').

This is fear-chills, not cold weather — for cold air use 춥다. The body-part partner 등골 collocates with 오싹하다 and 서늘하다, not 춥다 ('등골이 춥다' is unnatural). Also, 오싹하다 captures sudden fright; don't use it for general anxiety or unease — prefer 불안하다 for that.

mistakes: It's about fear/dread chills, not feeling physically cold from the weather — for cold air you want 춥다, not 등골이 오싹하다.
Pair 등골 with 오싹하다 or 서늘하다 — don't swap in 춥다 ('cold'); '등골이 춥다' is not idiomatic.
Don't replace it with bare 무섭다 ('scary') when you mean the physical shiver — 무섭다 names the feeling, 등골이 오싹하다 conveys the spine reaction.

english: to praise someone lavishly / can't stop praising (lit. 'the saliva in one's mouth dries up' — from talking so much)
usage: 엄마가 너 칭찬을 입에 침이 마르게 하더라.
Mom couldn't stop singing your praises.
Casual; usual frame 입에 침이 마르게 + 칭찬하다
사장님이 그 직원을 입에 침이 마르도록 칭찬하셨어요.
The boss praised that employee to no end.
Polite; 마르도록 ('to the point of drying') is a common form
다들 그 식당을 입에 침이 마르게 추천해.
Everyone recommends that restaurant nonstop.
Extends to enthusiastic recommendations (추천하다)
입에 침이 마르게 자랑하던데 진짜 좋은가 봐.
They bragged about it endlessly, so it must be really good.
With 자랑하다 = relentless bragging
examples: A: 선생님이 오늘 뭐라고 하셨어? / B: 네 그림을 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하셨어.
A: What did the teacher say today? / B: She praised your drawing to the skies, nonstop.
A/B exchange; lavish praise reported naturally
친구가 그 카페를 입에 침이 마르도록 얘기해서 가 봤어요.
My friend raved about that cafe so much that I finally went.
Praise leading to action; -아서 ('so') links cause to result
할머니는 손주 얘기만 나오면 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하세요.
Grandma gushes nonstop whenever her grandkids come up.
Real-situation habitual gushing; -세요 honorific for grandma; -만 나오면 = 'whenever ~ comes up'
nuance: Literally 'the saliva in one's mouth dries up' — talk up someone or something for so long that your mouth runs dry, conveying lavish, tireless, unstoppable praise. The dividing line from plain 칭찬하다 ('to praise') is intensity and duration: a single 'good job' is 칭찬하다, whereas 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하다 means gushing on and on without end. Crucially, this idiom almost never stands alone — it is an adverbial modifier that clamps onto a verb, nearly always 칭찬하다 ('praise'), 자랑하다 ('brag'), or 추천하다 ('recommend'), in the fixed adverbial forms 입에 침이 마르게 or 입에 침이 마르도록. The tone is warm, affectionate, and admiring — it is almost never used sarcastically. Register is casual-to-polite, appropriate from family to workplace storytelling. The English-speaker pitfalls: 이 idiom has nothing to do with literal thirst or dehydration ('dry mouth' as a medical symptom); thirst is 목이 마르다 ('my throat/neck is dry'), not 입에 침이 마르다, and mixing them causes real confusion.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 입 ('mouth') + 침 ('saliva') + 마르다 ('to dry up'), literally 'the saliva in one's mouth dries from talking so much.' 실제 뜻: to praise, brag about, or recommend something or someone lavishly and without stopping — the mouth works overtime until it runs dry.

Fits warm storytelling: a parent bragging about a child, a friend raving about a restaurant, a boss publicly lauding an employee. Tone is affectionate and admiring, never sarcastic. Casual to polite. Fine in family and work contexts. Not formal-written (use 극찬하다 'to lavish praise' in formal prose).

칭찬하다 ('to praise') is a single act — one compliment qualifies. 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하다 is relentless, sustained gushing. 극찬하다 ('to lavish praise') is the formal/written equivalent. 자화자찬하다 ('to praise oneself') is boasting, but this idiom covers praising others too.
Two adverbial forms are both natural: 입에 침이 마르게 (plainer, more common) and 입에 침이 마르도록 (slightly more literary/emphatic, 'to the point of drying'). Always followed by a verb: ~게/~도록 + 칭찬하다/자랑하다/추천하다.

Nothing to do with literal thirst or dry-mouth symptoms — for real thirst use 목이 마르다 ('my throat is dry'). Also, this idiom needs a partner verb: never drop 칭찬하다/자랑하다/추천하다 and let it stand alone, or it loses its meaning. Don't conjugate it as a completed action to describe one compliment — it lives in the adverbial -게/-도록 form.

mistakes: It means praising endlessly, not literally being thirsty or having a dry mouth — for real thirst use 목이 마르다 ('my throat is dry').
Don't drop the verb — it's used as 입에 침이 마르게/마르도록 + (칭찬하다/자랑하다/추천하다), not as a standalone statement.
Don't conjugate it as a finished action ('입에 침이 말랐다' to describe one compliment); it lives in the adverbial -게/-도록 form modifying the praising verb.

english: to work well together / be in sync as a team (lit. 'one's hands and feet match')
usage: 우리 둘은 손발이 잘 맞아.
The two of us work together really well.
Casual; 잘 ('well') is the usual partner adverb
새 팀이랑 손발이 맞아서 일이 수월해요.
I'm in sync with the new team, so work goes smoothly.
Polite; ~이랑 손발이 맞다 = 'in sync WITH ~'
손발이 안 맞아서 자꾸 실수가 나.
We're out of sync, so mistakes keep happening.
손발이 안 맞다 = the opposite
오래 같이 일하니까 손발이 척척 맞네.
We've worked together so long we're perfectly in sync.
척척 = 'smoothly, snappily,' an intensifying mimetic
examples: A: 오늘 행사 어땠어요? / B: 팀이랑 손발이 딱 맞아서 무사히 끝냈어요.
A: How did the event go? / B: We were perfectly in sync as a team so it finished without a hitch.
A/B exchange; 딱 맞다 = 'match exactly'; 무사히 = 'without incident'
주방이랑 홀이 손발이 맞아야 장사가 잘돼요.
The kitchen and the floor have to be in sync for business to run well.
Restaurant teamwork; -아야 = 'only if/when'
처음엔 손발이 안 맞았는데 이제 호흡이 잘 맞아요.
At first we were out of sync, but now we work in great harmony.
Real-situation arc; 호흡이 맞다 introduced as the close synonym for contrast
nuance: Literally 'hands and feet match,' it describes two or more people whose actions line up like a well-rehearsed team — the right rhythm where each anticipates what the other will do next. It is about working chemistry: coordinated task-timing, mutual anticipation, smooth handoffs. The dividing line from the near-synonym 호흡이 맞다 ('breathing matches') is subtle: both mean 'in sync,' but 손발이 맞다 stresses coordinated physical or operational action (who does what, when), while 호흡이 맞다 emphasizes an intuitive shared tempo or feel, and is especially common for performance partners or sports. Crucially, 손발이 맞다 is about professional/cooperative chemistry, NOT romantic compatibility or personality — for those use 잘 어울리다 or 궁합이 맞다. Register is casual-to-polite, ubiquitous at work, in sport, and whenever teamwork is the topic. The English-speaker pitfall: 'we match' or 'we get along' tempts learners to use it for personal affinity, but its domain is strictly shared action; and it is always mutual — mark the partner with ~와/과 or ~이랑.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 손 ('hands') + 발 ('feet') + 맞다 ('to match/fit'), literally 'hands and feet match.' 실제 뜻: two or more people work together in perfectly coordinated rhythm — each anticipates the other, tasks mesh without collision, teamwork flows.

Use it for work teams, restaurant kitchen-floor coordination, sports duos, project partners, any cooperative setting. Casual to polite. Safe between friends, coworkers, and in business contexts. Never in formal written reports — use 협업이 원활하다 ('cooperation proceeds smoothly') there.

호흡이 맞다 ('breathing matches') leans toward intuitive shared tempo — especially natural in performance or sport. 손발이 맞다 is more operational: who does what, timing of tasks. Both are positive; the choice is how you frame the sync. 잘 어울리다 / 궁합이 맞다 is for personality or romantic fit — not 손발이 맞다.
손발이 잘 맞다 (positive, 'work well together'), 손발이 안 맞다 (negative, 'out of sync'), 손발이 딱 맞다 ('match exactly, perfectly'). Intensifier mimetic 척척: 손발이 척척 맞다 ('work in perfect, snappy sync').

'We match' or 'we get along' tempts learners to use 손발이 맞다 for romantic or personality compatibility, but that belongs to 잘 어울리다 or 궁합이 맞다. 손발이 맞다 is strictly about coordinated action. It is inherently mutual — you cannot be 손발이 맞다 alone; mark the partner with ~와/과 or ~이랑.

mistakes: Use it for teamwork/coordination, not for romantic or personality compatibility — that's 잘 어울리다 or 궁합이 맞다.
It needs two or more people — you can't be 손발이 맞다 by yourself; the partner is marked with ~와/과 or ~이랑 ('in sync WITH ~').
Don't confuse it with 호흡이 맞다 carelessly: 손발 stresses coordinated actions/tasks, 호흡 stresses intuitive shared rhythm.

english: to actively step up and help / throw oneself into something wholeheartedly (lit. 'to take off one's shoes and step forward')
usage: 네가 발 벗고 나서 줘서 진짜 고마워.
Thank you for stepping up and really pitching in.
Casual; -아 주다 ('do it for me') adds the favor nuance
이웃들이 발 벗고 나서서 도와줬어요.
The neighbors went out of their way to help.
Polite; -아서 chains 'stepped up AND helped'
회사가 발 벗고 나서서 문제를 해결했어.
The company actively stepped in and solved the problem.
Subject can be an organization taking initiative
친구 일이라면 발 벗고 나서는 사람이야.
He's the type to drop everything to help a friend.
~라면 ('when it comes to ~'); describes a generous character
examples: A: 아무도 안 도와줘서 걱정이야. / B: 내가 발 벗고 나설게, 같이 하자.
A: Nobody's helping and I'm worried. / B: I'll roll up my sleeves and step in — let's do this together.
A/B exchange; B volunteers wholeheartedly; -ㄹ게 = commitment
선배가 발 벗고 나서서 취업을 도와줬어요.
A senior went all in to help me find a job.
Going above and beyond; shows the senior-junior helping dynamic common in Korean workplaces
그 문제는 아무도 발 벗고 나서지 않아서 오래 방치됐어요.
Nobody stepped up for that issue, so it was left alone for ages.
Real-situation negative — no one took initiative; 방치되다 = 'be left neglected'; shows the negative form
nuance: Literally 'to take off your shoes and step forward' — in old Korea shoes were valuable, so kicking them off to wade barefoot into a muddy task signalled 'I'm completely committed, no holding back.' The key distinction from plain 돕다 ('to help') is initiative and wholehearted energy: 돕다 can be passive or asked-for, but 발 벗고 나서다 highlights someone who volunteers of their own accord, going well out of their way. Compare 앞장서다 ('to take the lead, go in front'), which stresses being out front leading a group, while 발 벗고 나서다 stresses self-giving willingness regardless of rank or role. The tone is warm and approving — it is almost always a compliment for the helper. Register is casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfalls: write it as three orthographic words, 발 벗고 나서다 (not 발벗고 나서다), and because the idiom implies voluntary, eager involvement, avoid it for reluctant or coerced help — use 마지못해 돕다 ('reluctantly help') for that.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 발 ('foot/shoes') + 벗다 ('to take off') + 나서다 ('to step forward'), literally 'to take off one's shoes and step forward.' 실제 뜻: to voluntarily throw oneself into helping, with complete commitment and eagerness — going well out of one's way for another person.

Rooted in old Korean life: shoes (짚신/미투리) were valuable and not worn into muddy or dirty work. Kicking them off to wade in barefoot was a signal of total commitment — 'I am all in, nothing held back.' The image survives as a metaphor for self-sacrificing willingness.

Use when praising someone who stepped up voluntarily and energetically for another person: a senior helping a junior find work, neighbors helping with disaster relief, a friend dropping everything for you. Almost always a compliment for the helper. Casual to polite; fine across all relationships. Avoid having the helper say it about themselves — it sounds self-congratulatory; let others apply it to you.

돕다 ('to help') is neutral and covers any aid, asked or unasked. 발 벗고 나서다 specifies volunteer eagerness, going out of one's way. 앞장서다 ('to take the lead, go in front') means leading a group from the front — position matters. 발 벗고 나서다 emphasizes self-giving willingness regardless of position or rank.

The idiom is always three words: 발 벗고 나서다. Common extensions: 발 벗고 나서서 돕다 ('step up and help'), 발 벗고 나서 주다 ('step up as a favor to someone'), 발 벗고 나서지 않다 (negative: 'not step up'). Habitual form: 발 벗고 나서는 사람 ('the type of person who always steps up').

Write it as three separate words: 발 벗고 나서다 — not 발벗고 나서다. Because it implies voluntary, wholehearted effort, do not use it for reluctant or forced help (use 마지못해 돕다 instead). And don't reduce it to 앞장서다 ('lead') — leading a group is different from the self-sacrificing willingness this idiom highlights.

mistakes: Mind the spacing: 발 벗고 나서다, not 발벗고 나서다 — 발 and 벗고 are separate words.
It implies wholehearted, voluntary effort to help — don't use it for reluctant or forced help; for that, plain 도와주다 (with 마지못해 'reluctantly') fits better.
Don't reduce it to 앞장서다 ('take the lead'): leading a group is one thing, but 발 벗고 나서다 highlights self-giving willingness, not necessarily being out front.

english: to feel the weight of responsibility / feel heavily burdened (lit. 'one's shoulders are heavy')
usage: 책임이 커서 어깨가 무거워.
The responsibility is big, so I feel the weight of it.
Casual; 책임 ('responsibility') is the core partner noun
중요한 일을 맡아서 어깨가 무겁습니다.
I've taken on an important task, so I feel the responsibility.
Polite/formal -습니다; staple of work speeches and new-role announcements
가장으로서 어깨가 무거워요.
As the breadwinner, I carry a heavy load.
~로서 ('in the role of'); family responsibility framing
기대가 큰 만큼 어깨가 더 무거워.
The bigger the expectations, the heavier the burden.
~만큼 ('to the extent that') links expectation to pressure
examples: A: 팀장 맡았다면서요? / B: 네, 어깨가 무거워요. 열심히 해야죠.
A: I heard you took on the team lead role? / B: Yes, I feel the weight of it. I'll have to work hard.
A/B exchange; classic new-role acceptance speech formula
다들 나만 믿는다고 하니까 어깨가 무거워.
Everyone says they're counting on me, so I feel the weight of responsibility.
Pressure from others' trust; common before a big presentation or performance
큰 프로젝트를 혼자 맡아서 어깨가 너무 무거워요.
I'm handling a big project alone, so the burden feels heavy.
Real-situation: overloaded and under pressure; 혼자 ('alone') adds the isolation that deepens the weight
nuance: Literally 'shoulders are heavy,' this idiom expresses the psychological weight of responsibility or others' expectations pressing down on you — the dignified seriousness of a duty you have accepted. The dividing line from the near-synonym 부담스럽다 ('to feel burdened or pressured') is tone and dignity: 부담스럽다 can be mild and social (an expensive gift is 부담스럽다 because it obliges reciprocation), covering any degree of social discomfort, whereas 어깨가 무겁다 is a humble, almost noble admission that an important charge rests squarely on you — the expected phrase in acceptance speeches, new-role announcements, and earnest talks about duty. Its relief counterpart is 어깨가 가벼워지다 ('shoulders get lighter'). Core partner nouns are 책임 ('responsibility') and 기대 ('expectation'); core partner verb is 맡다 ('to take on'). Register covers casual through formal. The English-speaker pitfalls: this is emotional/responsibility weight, NOT literal shoulder pain (use 어깨가 결리다 or 아프다 for physical aches); and do not confuse it with 어깨가 처지다 ('shoulders droop'), which expresses dejection or discouragement rather than the weight of duty.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 어깨 ('shoulders') + 무겁다 ('to be heavy'), literally 'shoulders are heavy.' 실제 뜻: to feel the psychological weight of responsibility, duty, or others' expectations — the dignified acknowledgement that something important rests on you.

The go-to phrase in new-role acceptance speeches, promotions, project kick-offs, and earnest self-reflection about duty. Casual (어깨가 무거워) to formal written (어깨가 무겁습니다). Safe across all registers and social levels. Also used about others: 어깨가 무거운 자리 ('a post carrying heavy responsibility').

부담스럽다 ('to feel burdened/pressured') is broader and milder: a too-generous gift is 부담스럽다. 어깨가 무겁다 is the dignified, heavy-duty version — specifically about the weight of an important role or expectation, not social awkwardness. 어깨가 처지다 ('shoulders droop') means dejection, not responsibility.

Relief counterpart: 어깨가 가벼워지다 ('shoulders become lighter'). Stronger: 어깨가 짓눌리다 ('shoulders are crushed'). Collocate: 어깨가 무거운 자리 ('a position of heavy responsibility'). -아지다 form: 어깨가 무거워졌어요 ('the weight has grown').

This is emotional/responsibility weight, NOT physical shoulder pain — stiff or sore shoulders are 어깨가 결리다 / 어깨가 아프다. Don't confuse it with 어깨가 처지다 ('shoulders droop' = feeling dejected/down), which is a different emotion entirely. Also, 부담스럽다 cannot fully substitute here when you want the dignified 'weight of duty' nuance.

mistakes: It's about emotional/responsibility burden, not literal shoulder pain or stiffness — physical aches are 어깨가 결리다 / 어깨가 아프다.
Don't confuse it with 어깨가 처지다 ('shoulders droop'), which means feeling discouraged or dejected, not weighed down by duty.
Don't swap in 부담스럽다 when you want the dignified 'weight of duty' nuance; 부담스럽다 can sound merely uncomfortable or about an over-generous favor.

english: to be shameless / thick-skinned / have a lot of nerve (lit. 'one's face is thick')
usage: 걔 진짜 얼굴 두껍다, 또 부탁하네.
He's got some nerve — asking for a favor again.
Casual, mildly critical; 을/를 often dropped: 얼굴 두껍다
그런 부탁을 하다니 얼굴이 두꺼우시네요.
Asking for that takes a lot of nerve.
Polite but pointed; -시- here is sarcastically deferential
나도 좀 얼굴 두꺼워져야 하나 봐.
Maybe I need to grow a thicker skin.
Self-talk; -아지다 = 'become'; positive 'less self-conscious' sense
낯짝이 두꺼워서 미안한 줄을 몰라.
He's so brazen he doesn't even feel sorry.
낯짝/낯이 두껍다 = blunter, harsher variants
examples: A: 저 사람 또 왔어? 지난번에 그러고도? / B: 그러니까, 진짜 얼굴 두껍다.
A: That person came back? After what happened last time? / B: I know, seriously — what nerve.
A/B exchange; shared incredulity at someone's brazenness
그렇게 민폐 끼치고도 태연한 거 보면 얼굴 두껍다.
Causing all that trouble and staying calm — what nerve.
민폐(를) 끼치다 = 'to be a nuisance to others'; classic shamelessness scenario
면접 땐 얼굴이 좀 두꺼워야 떨지 않아요.
For interviews you need a bit of thick skin so you don't get nervous.
Real-situation positive flip: not easily flustered; shows the encouraging 'don't be shy' usage
nuance: Literally 'the face is thick,' it labels someone shameless or brazen — a person who feels no embarrassment where a normal person would. English has the parallel image 'thick-skinned,' but beware the register gap: English 'thick-skinned' is typically a compliment ('unbothered by criticism'), whereas Korean 얼굴이 두껍다 is most often mildly negative or teasing ('no shame'). It only flips positive in contexts like job interviews or public speaking — 얼굴 좀 두꺼워야 해 ('you need to be a bit bolder/less shy'). The dividing line from the near-synonym 뻔뻔하다 ('brazen, impudent') is register and sharpness: 뻔뻔하다 is the plain adjective and can sound flatly accusatory; 얼굴이 두껍다 is the idiomatic, often lighter or jokier phrasing between familiar people. Blunter, rougher variants: 낯이 두껍다, 낯짝이 두껍다; the noun for the trait is 철면피 (鐵面皮, 'iron-face skin'). Register is casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfall: it has nothing to do with literal facial skin thickness; and tone-awareness is essential — it can sting as an insult, so never say it bluntly to a superior.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 얼굴 ('face') + 두껍다 ('to be thick'), literally 'the face is thick.' 실제 뜻: shameless, brazen — lacking the embarrassment a situation calls for. Carries the idea that a thick face acts as armor against shame. Default tone is mildly negative or teasing; occasionally positive ('bold, not easily flustered').

Casual to polite; most common among friends commenting on someone audacious. In workplace chat it can sting, so use carefully with seniors or strangers. Fine as self-deprecating humor: '나 좀 얼굴 두꺼워져야겠어' ('I need to grow a thicker skin'). Avoid in formal or official speech — use 뻔뻔하다 in writing.

뻔뻔하다 ('brazen/impudent') is the plain adjective form and can sound directly accusatory. 얼굴이 두껍다 is idiomatic and often carries a joking or sighing tone. 낯짝이 두껍다 / 낯이 두껍다 are rougher, harsher synonyms. The Sino-Korean noun 철면피 (鐵面皮) means 'one who is completely shameless' — a more formal label.

Blunter variants: 낯이 두껍다, 낯짝이 두껍다 (harsher register). Noun form: 철면피 ('iron face'). Becoming/growing: 얼굴이 두꺼워지다 ('to become thicker-faced,' i.e. bolder or more brazen). Opposite: 얼굴이 얇다 (not common but exists: 'easily embarrassed').

English 'thick-skinned' is usually a compliment (unbothered by criticism); Korean 얼굴이 두껍다 is most often the negative 'shameless.' Nothing to do with literal facial skin. Tone matters: it can land as an insult, so never say it bluntly to a superior or in formal contexts. Map it carefully — it is not the same as 대담하다 ('to be bold') or 자신감이 있다 ('to be confident').

mistakes: Nothing to do with literal skin thickness on the face — it's about shamelessness, so a dermatology reading is wrong.
Tone matters: it can sound insulting, so don't say it bluntly to a superior or anyone you must stay polite with.
Don't assume it maps to the English compliment 'thick-skinned' (= unbothered by criticism); the default Korean sense is the negative 'shameless.'

english: to be incredibly busy / have no time to even breathe (lit. 'no moment to even open one's eyes and nose')
usage: 요즘 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바빠.
I'm so swamped these days I can't even catch a breath.
Casual; almost always with 바쁘다, joined by -이 (눈코 뜰 새 없이)
연말이라 눈코 뜰 새 없이 지내고 있어요.
It's year-end, so I'm run off my feet.
Polite; -고 있다 ('have been') for an ongoing hectic stretch
애 둘 키우느라 눈코 뜰 새가 없어.
Raising two kids leaves me no time to breathe.
새가 없다 form with subject 이/가
오픈 시간엔 눈코 뜰 새 없이 손님이 밀려와.
At opening time customers pour in nonstop.
밀려오다 = 'to flood in'; workplace rush scene
examples: A: 요즘 어때? / B: 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바빠서 밥도 제대로 못 먹어.
A: How are things lately? / B: I'm so slammed I can barely eat properly.
A/B exchange; 밥도 제대로 못 먹다 = 'can't even eat a proper meal,' a natural stacking phrase
행사 준비로 일주일 내내 눈코 뜰 새 없이 일했어.
I worked flat out all week preparing for the event.
일주일 내내 = 'all week long'; sustained, not one-off busyness
식당이 점심엔 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바빠서 정신이 하나도 없어요.
The restaurant is so slammed at lunch I can't think straight.
Real-situation: 정신이 없다 ('frazzled') stacks naturally; peak-hour restaurant rush
nuance: Literally 'no gap (새 = 사이, 'interval') to even open your eyes and nose,' it is a vivid hyperbole for being so frantically busy that you cannot spare a single second to breathe or collect yourself. The dividing line from plain 바쁘다 ('to be busy') is extreme intensity: 바쁘다 covers any degree of busyness, while 눈코 뜰 새 없다 sits at the absolute top — you can't even blink. It functions almost entirely as the set adverbial chunk 눈코 뜰 새 없이 + 바쁘다/일하다/지내다, which is why many textbooks treat 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바쁘다 as a fixed phrase. The alternative form 눈코 뜰 새가 없다 takes the subject 이/가. Note 새 here is the noun 사이/간격 ('gap, interval'), not the bird 새 ('bird') — that homophone trips beginners into a baffling literal image. Register is casual-to-polite, extremely common for any hectic stretch at work or home. The English-speaker pitfall: keep the exact spacing 눈코 뜰 새 없다 (눈코 is one compound word; 뜰 새 = 'a moment to open'); and don't deploy it for a calm 'I have no time' — there must be breathless, overwhelming busyness for this extreme hyperbole to fit.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 눈코 ('eyes and nose') + 뜰 새 ('a gap/moment to open') + 없다 ('there is none'). The image: so rushed you cannot even take a moment to open your eyes and nose — no time for even the most basic awareness. 실제 뜻: at the absolute peak of busyness, utterly overwhelmed.

Used for sustained, peak busy periods — year-end at work, restaurant rush hour, exam prep week, childcare overload. Casual to polite; safe with friends, coworkers, and bosses. Conveys vivid, almost humorous self-awareness about being swamped. Not for written formal reports — use 업무가 과중하다 ('workload is excessive') there.

바쁘다 ('to be busy') is the neutral, any-degree word. 눈코 뜰 새 없다 is extreme-hyperbole: you can't blink. 정신없이 바쁘다 ('frantically busy') is a close competitor but less idiom-vivid. 몸이 열 개라도 모자라다 ('even if I had ten bodies it wouldn't be enough') focuses on understaffing; 눈코 뜰 새 없다 focuses on sheer time pressure.
Adverbial form: 눈코 뜰 새 없이 + verb (most common). Subject form: 눈코 뜰 새가 없다. Common completions: 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바쁘다, 눈코 뜰 새 없이 일하다, 눈코 뜰 새 없이 지내다. Intensifier: 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바쁜 하루.

새 here is 사이/간격 ('gap/interval'), not 새 ('bird') — the homophone is a common source of confusion. Keep the correct spacing: 눈코 is one word, then 뜰 새 없다. Don't use it for a casual 'I don't have time' — it requires genuine, breathless busyness to justify the hyperbole.

mistakes: Keep the spacing 눈코 뜰 새 없다 (눈코 is one word; 뜰 새 = 'a moment to open') — not 눈 코 뜰새 없다.
It's an intensity phrase usually attached to 바쁘다 — don't use it for a neutral 'I have no time'; it requires real, breathless busyness.
새 here means 'gap/interval' (사이), not 새 ('bird') — don't let the homophone mislead your reading.

english: to get ripped off / be overcharged (lit. 'to wear a gourd dipper')
usage: 관광지에서 완전 바가지 썼어.
I got totally ripped off at the tourist spot.
Casual; 를 often dropped (바가지 쓰다); buyer overpays
택시 타다가 바가지 쓴 것 같아요.
I think I got overcharged in the taxi.
Polite; -ㄴ 것 같다 ('seems that') softens a suspicion
여기 비싸니까 바가지 쓰지 않게 가격 먼저 물어봐.
It's pricey here, so ask the price first to avoid getting fleeced.
-지 않게 ('so as not to'); practical advice
사장이 외국인한테 바가지를 씌웠어.
The owner ripped the foreigner off.
바가지(를) 씌우다 = the SELLER does the overcharging
examples: A: 그 시장 어땠어? / B: 흥정 안 했더니 완전 바가지 썼어.
A: How was that market? / B: I didn't haggle and totally got fleeced.
A/B exchange; 흥정 ('haggling') as the prevention; -더니 shows cause-and-effect regret
시세 모르고 샀다가 바가지 썼어.
I bought it without knowing the going rate and got overcharged.
시세 = 'market/going price'; -다가 marks the slip-up that led to the loss
축제 음식이 평소의 두 배라 바가지 쓴 기분이었어요.
The festival food was double the usual price — felt like a total ripoff.
Real-situation: inflated event pricing; 평소의 두 배 = 'double the usual price'; 기분이었다 ('felt like') adds subjectivity
nuance: Literally 'to wear (쓰다) a gourd dipper (바가지)' — in folk imagery an overloaded debt was said to be dumped on your head like a basinful of water, so 바가지를 쓰다 means being charged far above the fair market price, being gouged. It thrives in talk of tourist traps, open-air markets, unlicensed taxis, and festival stalls. The dividing line from plain 비싸다 ('expensive') is fairness: 비싸다 just means the price is high (possibly justified), whereas 바가지(를) 쓰다 implies you were charged ABOVE the fair going rate, unfairly. The crucial grammar pair you must learn: 바가지(를) 쓰다 = YOU, the buyer, got overcharged (쓰다 = to wear/put on — the gourd lands on your head); 바가지(를) 씌우다 = the SELLER dumps the gourd on someone (씌우다, causative 'to make wear'). Register is casual-to-polite, and 바가지 is also used as a standalone noun: '이건 바가지야' ('this is a ripoff'). The English-speaker pitfalls: reversing 쓰다 ('I got ripped off') and 씌우다 ('they ripped someone off') is a very common mistake; and do not use it for poor product quality — overcharge is strictly about price, not product.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 바가지 ('gourd dipper/basin') + 쓰다 ('to put on/wear'), literally 'to have a gourd placed on one's head.' 실제 뜻: to be charged far above the fair market price — to get gouged. The folk image is an overloaded debt or price being dumped on the buyer like a basinful of water.

Fits tourist areas, open markets, unlicensed taxis, festival stalls, unfamiliar repair shops — anywhere pricing is opaque or exploitative. Casual to polite. Fine to say to friends ('완전 바가지 썼어!') or in polite narrative ('바가지 쓴 것 같아요'). Also used as a preventive warning: 바가지 쓰지 않으려면 흥정해.

비싸다 ('expensive') is neutral — a Michelin-starred restaurant is 비싸다 but not 바가지. 바가지(를) 쓰다 means the price is specifically above fair market value in an exploitative way. 뜯기다 ('to get fleeced/taken') is a blunter synonym. The noun 바가지 alone as 이건 바가지야 means 'this is a ripoff.'

Buyer side: 바가지(를) 쓰다. Seller side: 바가지(를) 씌우다 ('to fleece/gouge someone'). Noun alone: 바가지 ('a ripoff'), 바가지요금 ('overcharge/gouge price'). Prevention phrase: 바가지 쓰지 않게 흥정하다 ('haggle to avoid getting ripped off').

Reversing 쓰다 ('got ripped off') and 씌우다 ('ripped someone off') is a very common error — keep the directionality: 쓰다 = the gourd lands ON YOU; 씌우다 = someone places the gourd ON ANOTHER. 바가지는 strictly about price, not product quality (use 별로다 / 안 좋다 for poor quality). And 비싸다 alone does not mean 바가지.

mistakes: Don't reverse the verbs: 쓰다 = you got ripped off; 씌우다 = the seller (or someone) ripped another person off.
It refers to being overcharged, not to a bad-quality product — for poor quality use 별로다 / 안 좋다.
Don't substitute plain 비싸다 ('expensive'): high price alone isn't 바가지; the nuance is being gouged ABOVE the fair rate.

english: you won't get anything out of it / there'll be nothing in it for you (often a warning or threat) (lit. 'there's not even broth')
usage: 한 번만 더 늦으면 국물도 없어.
Be late one more time and you'll get nothing from me.
Casual warning/threat; -으면 ('if') sets the condition
약속 안 지키면 국물도 없을 줄 알아.
If you break the promise, don't expect anything good.
Half-joking threat; -을 줄 알아 = 'you'd better know / be warned'
이번에 도와줘도 나한테 국물도 없더라.
Even though I helped this time, I got nothing out of it.
-아도 ('even if'); complaining about zero payoff
그렇게 해 봤자 너한테 국물도 없어.
Even if you do that, there's nothing in it for you.
-아 봤자 ('no matter how much you ~'); framing a pointless effort
examples: A: 저한테 뭔가 좀 돌아오나요? / B: 이번엔 국물도 없어, 그냥 해.
A: Is there anything in it for me? / B: Nothing this time — just do it.
A/B exchange; casual, blunt refusal of any payoff
밤새 도왔는데 고맙단 말도 없고, 정말 국물도 없네.
I helped all night and didn't even get a thanks — nothing to show for it.
Zero reward after significant effort; resigned -네 ending
사장님이 또 실수하면 국물도 없다고 하셨어요.
The boss said if it happens again there'll be no mercy.
Workplace warning relayed with -다고 하다; shows it is reportable in polite speech
nuance: Literally 'there isn't even broth (국물)' — picture a shared pot of stew scraped so clean that not a single drop of soup remains for you, so 국물도 없다 means there is absolutely nothing to be gained: no share, no benefit, no leftover mercy. Its most common use is as a half-joking but pointed warning from someone with the upper hand: 한 번만 더 그러면 국물도 없어 ('do that once more and you'll get nothing from me'). A second use is grumbling that effort yielded zero reward ('도와줬는데 국물도 없더라'). The dividing line from the threat-phrase 가만 안 두다 ('I won't let it slide') is what is threatened: 가만 안 두다 threatens active punishment, whereas 국물도 없다 threatens total withholding of any goodwill or payoff — the carrot disappears rather than a stick appearing. Register is firmly casual and the phrasing can sting, so it suits friends, family, or clearly informal settings — never in professional or deferential speech. The English-speaker pitfalls: 국물 here is NOT literal soup — it means 'leftover benefit/share'; and the implied subject is 'you' or 'there will be none for you,' so the sentence is essentially shorthand for 너한테 돌아오는 것이 국물도 없다.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 국물 ('broth/soup') + 도 없다 ('not even … exists'), literally 'there isn't even broth left.' 실제 뜻: there is absolutely nothing to be gained — no benefit, no share, no payoff, no mercy. The image is a shared pot scraped completely clean; you get not a drop.

Two main settings: (1) Half-joking warning from someone with leverage — 한 번만 더 그러면 국물도 없어 — among friends, family, or a parent to a child. (2) Grumbling that an effort went unrewarded — 도와줬는데 국물도 없더라. Firmly casual; never polite or professional speech. If you must convey the same idea at work, say 혜택이 전혀 없습니다 ('there are no benefits whatsoever').

가만 안 두다 ('I won't let it slide') threatens active punishment — a stick. 국물도 없다 threatens withholding any goodwill — the carrot vanishes. 得도 없다 (formal written) and 건질 게 없다 ('nothing to salvage') are near-synonyms in the 'no payoff' sense but lack the pointed warning edge.

Condition + threat: -으면 국물도 없어 ('if ~, you'll get nothing'). Even-if frame: -아도/-아 봤자 국물도 없어. Softer: 뭔가 돌아오는 게 없다 ('nothing comes back to you'). Standalone noun: 국물 = 'a share, a cut': 국물 좀 줘 ('give me a cut/share').

국물 here is NOT literal soup — it is figurative 'leftover benefit/payoff/share.' Don't picture food. Because the tone is so informal and can sting, never use it in polite or professional contexts. Also note the implied 'for you': the full thought is 너한테 돌아오는 국물도 없다, so it is personal and pointed, not just a statement about scarcity.

mistakes: Nothing to do with actual soup — 국물 here means 'leftover benefit/payoff/share,' not broth you can drink.
The threatening tone is informal and can sound harsh; don't use it in polite or professional contexts where you must stay deferential.
It threatens WITHHOLDING any reward or mercy, not active punishment — for 'I'll make you pay' use 가만 안 두다, not 국물도 없다.

english: to throw cold water on something / ruin the mood or kill the momentum (lit. 'to pour cold water over')
usage: 분위기 좋았는데 걔가 찬물을 끼얹었어.
The mood was great but he threw cold water on it.
Casual; 분위기 ('mood/vibe') is the classic object being ruined
좋은 소식에 찬물을 끼얹고 싶진 않지만요.
I don't mean to rain on the good news, but…
Polite hedge before delivering bad news; -지만 = 'but'
다들 신났는데 그 말 한마디가 찬물을 끼얹었어요.
Everyone was excited, but that one comment killed it.
말 한마디 = 'a single remark' as the subject; one-word buzzkill
계획에 자꾸 찬물 끼얹지 말고 좀 응원해 줘.
Stop pouring cold water on the plan and cheer me on.
-지 말다 ('don't'); 을 dropped colloquially
examples: A: 다들 여행 가자고 신났었는데. / B: 근데 민준이가 찬물을 끼얹어서 분위기가 식었어.
A: Everyone was hyped about the trip. / B: But Minjun threw cold water on it and the vibe died.
A/B exchange; 분위기가 식다 = 'the mood cooled/died' pairs naturally
회의 분위기가 살아나려는데 부장님이 찬물을 끼얹었어요.
The meeting was warming up, but the manager threw cold water on it.
-려는데 = 'just as it was about to'; workplace momentum killed by a senior comment
축하 자리에 굳이 찬물을 끼얹는 말을 할 필요는 없잖아.
There's no need to say something that ruins a celebration.
Real-situation: 굳이 ('needlessly/without cause') + advice to be tactful; shows the disapproving framing
nuance: Literally 'to pour cold water over (something hot),' it means to suddenly and actively kill an upbeat mood, rising excitement, or building momentum — typically with a negative remark or unwelcome news, like dousing a warm fire. The key dividing line from the near-synonym 김(을) 빼다 / 김새다 ('to let the steam out / deflate') is agency: 김새다 describes excitement that fizzles on its own with no clear culprit, whereas 찬물을 끼얹다 firmly points the finger at an active party who chose to throw the buzzkill. For the expression to land correctly, there must be heat to douse — enthusiasm, a rising vibe, a plan people were excited about — so do not apply it to neutral situations. Partners: 분위기에 ('to the mood'), 좋은 소식에 ('to good news'), 계획에 ('to a plan'). Register is casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfalls: the verb 끼얹다 is frequently misspelled — it carries the ㄶ batchim (끼얹-, romanized kki-eon-da), so avoid 끼언다 or 끼엊다; and the phrase requires a target atmosphere to ruin, so never use it where there was no positive mood to begin with.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 찬물 ('cold water') + 끼얹다 ('to pour/splash over'), literally 'to pour cold water over.' 실제 뜻: to actively kill an upbeat mood, rising excitement, or building momentum — like suddenly dousing a warm fire with cold water. The key: something must be 'hot' (excited, positive) before the cold water lands.

Used when a single remark, news item, or person kills an enthusiastic atmosphere: a fun plan deflated, a meeting momentum broken, a celebration disrupted. Casual to polite. Fine with friends and in workplace storytelling. The expression carries mild reproach for the buzzkill — use it to describe, not to lecture someone in their face (try 분위기 파악 좀 해 'read the room' for that).

김새다 / 김이 빠지다 ('steam escapes / deflates'): the excitement fizzles without a clear culprit — it just happens. 찬물을 끼얹다 points to a specific active agent who threw the buzzkill. 분위기를 망치다 ('to ruin the atmosphere') is a broader, plainer phrasing; 찬물을 끼얹다 is the vivid idiomatic version.
Subject flexibility: 그 말이/그 사람이 찬물을 끼얹다. Target marked with 에: 분위기에/계획에/축하 자리에 찬물을 끼얹다. Object 을 frequently dropped colloquially: 찬물 끼얹다. Noun phrase: 찬물을 끼얹는 말 ('a buzzkill remark').

끼얹다 carries the ㄶ batchim (pronounce kki-eon-da) — commonly misspelled as 끼언다 or 끼엊다. The expression requires a target positive mood to ruin; don't apply it to neutral situations. Don't blur it with 김새다 ('to fizzle on its own') — 찬물을 끼얹다 points the finger at an active buzzkill, not natural deflation.

mistakes: Spelling: it's 찬물을 끼얹다 (끼얹- has the ㄶ batchim, read 'kki-eon'), not 끼언다 or 끼엊다.
It implies actively spoiling a POSITIVE mood, so don't use it for just any bad news; there must be enthusiasm or momentum to ruin.
Don't blur it with 김새다 ('to fizzle'): 김새다 is the excitement deflating on its own, while 찬물을 끼얹다 points the finger at a deliberate buzzkill.
